4 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)¶

  • CNNs are a type of neural network that excels at image processing.

  • In addition to height information, species information is critical for understanding regeneration success.

  • Current regeneration monitoring systems rely on a combination of photo-intepretation and field surveys to record tree species at the stand and plot-level, respectively.

  • However, the efficiency of species indentification could be increased by training models to automatically classify tree species in remotely sensed data.

  • In this example, we will train a CNN to classify the species of images individual tree crowns.

    • Our trained CNN can be saved and later deployed to automatically perform species classification.

Figure 5. ITC selected for this example. Note that not all trees in the image were selected. There are some small ITC that were excluded for simplicity.

About the data¶

  • Trees were identified in the field and their species information was later associated with drone imagery.
  • Bounding boxes were drawn around ITC in the imagery.
  • The bounding boxes were then used to clip the imagery, creating small images equal to the extent of each box.
  • We collected the path of each image as well as the species of the tree in each image in a csv file.

Before we get into building our CNN, let's learn about what makes CNNs different from the DNN we built earlier.

4.1 Convolutions¶

Where the DNN we build earlier transformed each row of an input table to make predictions, CNNs transform input imagery to do the same.

The way they do this is through convolutions.

Figure 5. Convolving an image.

  • Convolutions are carried out with kernels.

  • Kernels are sliding windows of fixed dimensions. The kernel in Figure 5 has a dimension of 3 x 3.

  • Each cell within a kernel has a value.

  • As the kernel slides across an image, it takes the dot product of it's values and the image pixels that the kernel overlays.

  • The dot product value is stored as a pixel in a newly created image.

  • The kernel then slides into a new position.

  • This sliding across the image is referred to as convolving.

  • Because the kernel cannot slide outside the bounds of the image, the product of convolution is smaller in dimension than the input.

    • In this example, we started with a 5x5 pixel image and ended with a new image with the dimensions 3x3 pixels.

  • With CNN, the weights of each node are equal to that node's kernel values.

    • So, as a CNN trains, it updates the configuration of its kernels to reveal more meaningful patterns.
    • Kernels in the first layers usually reveal simple patterns such as edges or curves.
    • Kernels in deeper layers reveal more nuanced patterns, such as faces or body parts.

  • The images produced by convolution are often referred to as Feature Maps.

    • This is because each image will reveal features of the targets the CNN is trying to classify.
    • We can then understand that the role of convolutional layers is to extract features from input images or to perform Feature Extraction.

4.2 Convolutions on RGB Imagery¶

Figure 6. Convolution on RGB Imagery.

  • Most images are comprised of three image channels: red, green, and blue - otherwise known as RGB.
  • When RGB imagery is used with CNN, separate kernels are learned for and applied to each image channel.
  • In this case, the filter of a node in a CNN is actually comprised of 3 kernels, one for each image channel.
  • For RGB imagery, the process of convolution occurs as in Figure 5 for each channel of an image.
  • This produces 3 new images, one for each channel.
  • These images are then combined by pixel-wise addition to create a final new image, the convolution output.

4.3 Pooling¶

Figure 7. Max Pooling

  • Most images are much larger than the 5x5 pixel examples used in Figures 5 and 6.
  • Because each node in a CNN layer will produce a new image and because each layer is likely to at least 32 nodes, CNNs consume a lot of memory for image storage.
  • To reduce memory load while preserving information, it is common to employ a technique called Pooling, whereby a kernel is used to further reduce the dimensions of convolutional outputs.
  • Figure 7 shows Max Pooling, where the maximum value within the kernel is used to build a new image.
  • In Figure 7, a 2x2 kernel is used for max pooling.
  • Other types of pooling are used with CNN, though max pooling is the most common.
    • Another example is average pooling, where the average value within a kernel is used to create a new image of reduced dimension.

Figure 8. An overview so far.

  • Input images are transformed with convolutional filters

  • Each node in the CNN will yield a new, unique image.

  • The dimensions of these images will be smaller than the inputs as a result of convolution.

  • Max pooling is applied to reduce memory load, creating new images of reduced dimensions.

  • The outputs of the first max pooling operation will become the inputs for the next convolutional layer and so on...

4.4 The Flatten Layer¶

Figure 9. Flatten.

  • After the last convolutional and pooling layers, Feature Extraction is complete.
  • Now, it is time to classify the extracted features.
  • To do this, each image in the max pooling output is flattened and combined so as to produce a 1-dimensional vector.
    • This is done row-by-row, image-by-image.

4.5 Fully Connected Layers¶

Figure 10. CNN Overview.

  • The flattened layer then becomes input for a Fully Connected Network.
  • The fully connected network is conceptually the same as the DNN we built earlier, wherein each layer is fully connected with the next.
  • The main difference is that instead of rows from a dataframe, it takes the flattened layer of each input image as its input.

Figure 11. Dropout.

  • As mentioned earlier, when trying to optimize their loss scores, neural networks can Overfit on their training sets.

  • This means that to improve their training loss scores, the networks begin to memorize the training data, rather than learning a generalized solution.

  • One mechanism used to prevent overfitting is Dropout, wherein nodes are randomly eliminated from the network during each epoch, forcing the network to find more generalized solutions.

5.2 Image Generators¶

  • We will use image generators to train our CNN
  • This will allow us to perform data augmentation

5.2.1 Normalization¶

  • Just as we normalized our data in the first example, we will do the same here by rescaling the pixel values of our images to ensure they are in a range between 0 and 255.
  • This is performed at Line 2 for our training data and at Line 11 for our testing data.

5.2.2 Data Augmentation¶

  • We have mentioned the problem of overfitting before

  • One approach to prevent overfitting with CNNs is to augment our training data.

  • This means that whenever the CNN loads a training image, it will perform random alterations or augmentations to that image so as to make it appear different from the original.

  • Image augmentation is particularly useful because as the CNN trains, it will be repeatedly exposed to the training data.

  • By introducing random augmentations to the training images each time they are loaded, they appear slightly different each time they are loaded, which allows the CNN to develop more generalized solutions to the classification problem.

    • This helps the CNN make accurate predictions on data it has not yet seen.

  • For example, rotation is a common data augmentation.

    • We specify at Line 3 that when the CNN loads a training image, it will perform a random rotation between 0 and 45 degrees.

  • Line 4 we specify that when the CNN loads a training image, it will shift the pixel values of the image to the left or right.

  • The value of 0.2 specifies that it will randomly shift the image between 0 and 20% of the total number of horizontal pixels

  • For example, if an image has a width of 100 pixels, the CNN will randomly shift those pixel values by up to 20 pixels to the left or right.

  • Image regions withon pixel values will have values of 0.

  • Similarly, at Line 5 we specify that the CNN will randomly zoom in by up up to 20%

  • Line 6: We specify that the CNN will randomly flip half of the training images.

  • Line 7: Here we specify that 20% of the training subset will be reserved as validation data.

  • Note that we do not perform augmentation on the test data.

  • We want to keep this data in its original form in order to guage the CNN's performance.

In [ ]:
train_generator = tf.keras.preprocessing.image.ImageDataGenerator(
    rescale = 1./255,
    rotation_range=45,
    width_shift_range=0.2,
    zoom_range=0.2,
    horizontal_flip=True,
    validation_split = 0.2
)

test_generator = tf.keras.preprocessing.image.ImageDataGenerator(
    rescale = 1./255
)

5.2.3 Reading in our data¶

  • Now that we have defined the parameters of our data generators, we can use them to read our data.

  • We will use the flow_from_dataframe function to do this.

    • Line 1: We create a variable named train_images to store our training images
    • Line 2: Specify the dataframe
    • Line 3: Specify the column containing the image file paths
    • Line 4: Specify the column containing the values we are predicting
    • Line 5: Here we specify the target size.
      • This is important because our images vary in dimension and the CNN requires that all images be of the same dimension.
      • By specifying the dimenions 120, 120, we tell the data generator to resize input images so that they are 120 x 120 pixels in dimension.
    • Line 6: Specify that our images are have three bands in the RGB format.
    • Line 7: 'raw' Specifies that the y_col (the variable we are predicting) contains the actual values we want to predict.
    • Line 8: A Batch refers to the number of images that the CNN will use for each weight update - 32 specifies that 32 images will be used for each update.
    • Using a Batch Size that is less than the size of the training dataset helps to conserve memory.
    • However, if the batch size is too small, weight updates may not represent the entire dataset and it may be difficult for the CNN to find a generalized solution.
    • Line 9: Specify that the order of the training data is to be randomly shuffled.
      • This also helps to prevent overfitting.
    • Line 10: Here we set a seed for the random shuffle so that we can repeat our analysis.
    • Line 11: Specify that the variable train_images will belong to our training subset, which we specified when we defined the train_generator in the cell above.

  • The same settings are applied to our validation images and our test images.

    • Note that we will not shuffle our validation images.
In [ ]:
train_images = train_generator.flow_from_dataframe(
    dataframe=train_df,
    x_col='Filepath2',
    y_col='Species',
    target_size=(120,120),
    color_mode='rgb',
    class_mode='raw',
    batch_size=32,
    shuffle=True,
    seed=42,
    subset='training'
)

val_images = train_generator.flow_from_dataframe(
    dataframe=train_df,
    x_col='Filepath2',
    y_col='Species',
    target_size=(120,120),
    color_mode='rgb',
    class_mode='raw',
    batch_size=32,
    shuffle=True,
    seed=42,
    subset='validation'
)

test_images = train_generator.flow_from_dataframe(
    dataframe=test_df,
    x_col='Filepath2',
    y_col='Species',
    target_size=(120,120),
    color_mode='rgb',
    class_mode='raw',
    batch_size=32,
    shuffle=False
)

5.3 Building our CNN¶

  • As in the previous example, we will use the Keras Sequential API.
  • Line 2: Here we define our first convolutional layer.
  • We specify that:
    • it will have 32 filters (nodes)
    • The kernel size of each filter is 3 x 3 pixels
    • The shape of the input data is 120 x 120 pixels with 3 image channels
    • We will use the 'relu' activation function.
  • Line 3: Here we define our pooling layer:
    • We will use max pooling with a kernel size of 2 x 2 pixels.
  • Lines 5-9 For this lines, we repeat the same structure for subsequent layers.
    • Note that for the 3rd layer, we specify 64 nodes instead of 32.

This concludes the feature extraction portion of our CNN.

  • Line 11: Here we define our flatten layer.

  • Line 12: Define our dense layer for classification

  • Line 14: Define our dropout.

    • This specifies that 50% of the Dense layer's nodes will randomly be disabled during each training epoch.

  • Line 16: Define our output layer, a dense layer with a size of 1.

    • For this layer, we will use the sigmoid activation function, which will transform values be between 0 and 1.
    • The actual values of the output layer will represent the likelihood of the prediction being a 0 (lodgepole pine) or a 1 (white spruce).
      • For example, if the output layer produces a value of 0.001, it is fairly certain that the image is of a lodgepole pine crown.
      • An output value of 0.45 can be interpreted as the CNN being somewhat unsure as to which class the crown belongs to, but leaning towards lodgepole pine.

  • Lines 19-21: Compile our model.

  • Line 19: specify binary cross entropy as our loss function

  • Line 20: use the adam optimizer

  • Line 21: track accuracy during training.

[NOTE: add more info on binary cross entropy, adam, and accuracy]

In [ ]:
model = Sequential()
model.add(Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=(3, 3), input_shape=(120, 120, 3), activation='relu'))
model.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

model.add(Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu'))
model.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

model.add(Conv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu'))
model.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

model.add(Flatten())
model.add(Dense(64, activation='relu'))

model.add(Dropout(0.5))

model.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))


model.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy',
              optimizer='adam',
              metrics=['accuracy'])

5.4 Training our CNN¶

  • We will use the same training parameters as we did in our first example:
  • 1000 training epochs and an early callback patience of 100 epochs.
In [ ]:
history = model.fit(
    train_images,
    validation_data=val_images,
    epochs=1000,
    callbacks=[
        tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
            monitor='val_loss',
            patience=100,
            restore_best_weights=True
        )
    ]
)

5.5 Plot the training history¶

In [ ]:
loss = history.history['loss']
val_loss = history.history['val_loss']
epochs = range(1, len(loss) + 1)
plt.plot(epochs, loss, 'y', label='Training loss')
plt.plot(epochs, val_loss, 'r', label='Validation loss')
plt.title('Training and validation loss')
plt.xlabel('Epochs')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.legend()
plt.show()


acc = history.history['accuracy']
val_acc = history.history['val_accuracy']
plt.plot(epochs, acc, 'y', label='Training accuracy')
plt.plot(epochs, val_acc, 'r', label='Validation accuracy')
plt.title('Training and validation accuracy')
plt.xlabel('Epochs')
plt.ylabel('Accuracy')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

5.6 Save the trained model¶

  • Our model took a while to train.
  • We will save it so that it can be loaded in the future without the need to perform training again.
In [ ]:
model.save(r'/content/drive/MyDrive/sub_test/sp_model_alt.h5')

WARNING:absl:You are saving your model as an HDF5 file via `model.save()` or `keras.saving.save_model(model)`. This file format is considered legacy. We recommend using instead the native Keras format, e.g. `model.save('my_model.keras')` or `keras.saving.save_model(model, 'my_model.keras')`.
